measurement: ratio: 1.57:1 (backswing 0.450s / downswing 0.287s), range 1.35-1.83, observed in 1 of 1 swings
plain: Your driver swing takes about half a second going back and a bit under a third of a second coming down — a rhythm of roughly 1.6 to 1. The timing itself is solid, because the strike is clearly audible and I could pin it to the frame. But this is the first swing of yours on record, so there is nothing yet to say whether that rhythm suits you. It is here as a starting point: if a later video comes back noticeably quicker or slower, that change will mean something.
note: Baseline only -- first video on record, so there is nothing to compare this against and no claim is made about whether 1.57:1 is good. Recorded so a later video can be checked against it. Timestamps: takeaway starts between 0.667s and 0.700s (club still at the ball at 0.667, clearly moving by 0.700); top at 1.133s, taken from the minimum of a player-cropped frame-difference series rather than by eye, since the arms are near-stationary for several frames there; impact at 1.420s from the audio transient (99x prominence), independently corroborated by the cropped-motion peak at 1.399-1.433s. The range reflects one-frame uncertainty at each end -- a ratio built from two sub-half-second durations is more sensitive to that than the raw numbers look.

measurement: holds the finish from ~1.8s to the clip's end at 2.97s (~1.1s) with no step, stumble, or recovery adjustment; observed in 1 of 1 swings
plain: You hold your finish for about a second after the ball is gone, with no step or stumble to catch yourself. This one I could only eyeball — I tried to put a number on it and the measurement failed, because the wind was moving the reeds behind you about as much as your body was moving. So treat it as a real observation but not a measured one. Nothing to work on here; it is the kind of thing worth not losing.
note: Eyeballed from a filmstrip, NOT quantified -- an attempt to back it with a player-cropped frame-difference series failed and should not be repeated blind on outdoor footage like this. The settled-finish median (1.42) sat inside the range of the backswing's own values (1.5-2.3) with excursions to 2.70, because wind-blown reeds behind the player and handheld camera shake put the noise floor at the same level as the body motion being measured. The visual observation stands on its own; there is no number behind it.

measurement: magnitude: 31.4px, noiseFloor: 2px (of which vertical rise 20.3px = 0.28 head-heights), observed in 1 of 1 swings measured
plain: In the one swing I could measure, your head finished about a quarter of a head-height higher at impact than it was at address. I am fairly confident the rise is real — the camera was steady enough to rule out shake as the cause. I am less confident about exactly how much, partly because some of it is your head turning to look toward the target rather than lifting, and partly because it is a single swing: the rest of the movement in that clip turned out to be walking and camera handling, not more swings. I would not change anything on this alone. If it shows up again in a second video, the usual work is keeping your chest over the ball a beat longer through impact.
note: Range session, 2026-07-04 clip, swing at 9.6-10.5s. Head crown tracked from address (9.600s) to impact (10.450s), corrected for camera drift using two static treeline silhouette tips; the two references agreed to within 0.245px, so the camera was near-still and the noise floor fell back to the 2px click-precision floor. Signal is 15.7x that floor. Baseline only -- assessment is neutral because this project carries no population baseline by design, so there is no basis to call 0.28 head-heights a fault; it is recorded so a later video can be compared via isImprovement. Scale: expressed in head-heights (crown-to-chin 73px at address) rather than inches, because the only known-size object in frame is the ball, which sits further from the camera than the head and would therefore inflate any inch conversion -- toInches correctly returned null. TWO CAVEATS. (1) Impact frame accuracy dominates this measurement: at 10.500s, one 0.033s frame later, the same rise reads 53.5px (0.73 head-heights) -- 33 of those pixels accumulate in that single post-impact frame as the body stands up naturally through the follow-through. 10.450s was chosen because it is the last frame with the ball still on the mat. Measuring one frame late would have overstated this finding by 2.6x. (2) The head also rotates toward the target between the two frames, so the topmost silhouette point is not guaranteed to be the same anatomical point; some share of the 20.3px is rotation rather than translation, making this an upper bound on true vertical rise. SPOT-CHECK FOR CONSISTENCY (2026-09-14): the source clip is 47.7s and has motion elsewhere in it -- camera handling/walking at 13.7-17s, a change of location (tee box to a range mat) with the camera going nearly empty around 30-33s, the golfer bending down to pick something up around 32-34s, a weak and ambiguous bump around 43-44s, and the recording being stopped by hand at 45.7-47.3s (an iOS control panel is visible in frame). Checked each visually; none is a second complete address-to-impact swing. This clip contains exactly one measurable swing, not several -- the user's same-club claim across swings could not be cross-checked against a second swing because there is not one to check it against. This is an honest absence of contradiction, not confirmed consistency.
